    DevDesk only ever spoke to docker. The first step toward podman support
    (§3.67) is to make the engine a value rather than a literal, so the
    packages that drive it can read one answer instead of each hardcoding
    "docker".
    
    internal/engine carries a Shape per engine: the binary, the credential
    helper prefix, the registry auth file, the host socket, and the --format
    templates. It is its own package rather than a field of internal/docker
    because internal/scan needs the same answer and does not import
    internal/docker — the internal/forge arrangement, where the thing every
    caller shares does not live inside one of its callers.
    
    Four things are deliberate:
    
    - Resolve() refuses a pinned engine that is absent instead of falling
      back to the other one. The two do not hold the same containers, so a
      silent substitution would answer a question nobody asked. That is
      credentials.Select's rule (§3.9).

      Getting that wrong costs the auth file location, not the invocation,
      so anything unrecognisable is treated as docker.

      today. That is the honest state: podman implements --format, but field
      equality is guaranteed nowhere, and no measurement has been taken —
      there is no podman on the machine this was written on. A divergence
      produces wrong rows rather than an error, so the indirection is there
      to make the fix one line instead of a refactor.
    - ParsesSystemDFVerbose is false for podman. `system df -v` is scraped by
      column offsets taken from a header line, and a value sliced out of the
      wrong column reads as data where a blank reads as an absence.

1	# DevDesk
2	
3	A terminal-based DevSecOps workstation built with Go and [Bubble Tea](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea). DevDesk centralizes the tools a developer needs daily — GitLab or GitHub, Docker, security scanning, and system monitoring — in a single keyboard-driven TUI.
4	
5	| | |
6	|---|---|
7	| **Dashboard** | Forge stats, Docker usage, OCI images, tool availability, service health |
8	| **Forge Explorer** | Browse and clone GitLab or GitHub, one backend per context |
9	| **Workspaces** | Local repositories with branch, status, last scan at a glance |
10	| **Security** | Trivy (CVE, secrets, licenses, misconfig) and Gitleaks scans |
11	| **Containers & OCI** | Manage running containers, browse and scan images |
12	| **Network Diagnostics** | DNS, ICMP, traceroute, TCP/HTTP/TLS checks, live port monitor |
13	
14	## Where to start
15	
16	This site follows the [Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/) documentation framework: each section answers a different kind of question.
17	
18	| Section | Answers | Start here if… |
19	|---|---|---|
20	| [Tutorial](tutorial/first-session.md) | "Show me, step by step" | You've never run DevDesk before |
21	| [How-to guides](how-to/install.md) | "How do I do *this specific thing*?" | You know DevDesk and need to accomplish a task |
22	| [Reference](reference/commands.md) | "What's the exact name/value/key?" | You need to look something up |
23	| [Explanation](explanation/index.md) | "Why does it work this way?" | You want to understand the design, or you're contributing code |
24	
25	## Requirements
26	
27	- Go 1.25.5+ (to build from source)
28	- A terminal with [Nerd Font](https://www.nerdfonts.com/) support — icons are used throughout the UI
29	- Optional, feature degrades gracefully if absent: [Trivy](https://trivy.dev/), [Gitleaks](https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks), Docker
30	
31	## Source
32	
33	DevDesk is developed at [github.com/anthnel/devdesk](https://github.com/anthnel/devdesk). Issues and pull requests are welcome — see [Contributing](contributing.md).
34

1	# Workspaces
2	
3	The `ws` view lists local repositories and plain directories side by side, and lets you scan and sync git repositories in place. This page explains the reasoning behind its file icons and its sync behavior — the "why", not a field-by-field reference.
4	
5	## The leftmost column: what a row *is*
6	
7	Each row in `ws` starts with a glyph naming what the entry **is**: a git repository, a directory, or a plain file. This replaced an earlier column that answered a different question — whether a directory looked like a *project* (by sniffing for `go.mod` or `package.json`) — which wasn't useful enough to keep as a whole column.
8	
9	The repository glyph is the one that earns its place: most of the row's actions (scan, sync, delete, open) only apply to git repositories, and shortcuts that don't apply get greyed out. Without a visual cue for "this is a repository," the user watches keys dim with nothing on the row explaining why.
10	
11	A few implementation notes worth knowing if you're extending the icon table:
12	
13	- **Basename is checked before extension.** `Dockerfile` has no extension at all, and `Dockerfile.dev` has `.dev`, which matches nothing — so an extension-first lookup would misclassify both.
14	- **Icons are colored by role, not by file type.** Coloring by file type (the way tools like `eza` do) tells you nothing actionable — `.go` vs `.rs` doesn't change what you can do with the file. Coloring by *role* (repository / directory / file) mirrors the same three-way split the action-availability logic already uses, so the color anticipates what the shortcut row is about to say.
15	- **Icons don't get invented for uncertain cases.** File types without a clearly appropriate glyph (`.kt`, `.scala`, `.hs`, `.zig`, `.tf`, …) fall back to a generic code-file icon rather than guessing.
16	- **The icon column carries no title and isn't searchable or sortable** — it adds no text a user could type, so filtering stays scoped to name and remote.
17	
18	A git repository is given the *same* visual role wherever DevDesk shows one — in `ws`, in the security inventory, and in the forge explorer. One object, one color, across three otherwise-unrelated views.
19	
20	## Syncing workspaces
21	
22	The sync action (`F`) fetches a repository and fast-forwards it if it's safe to do so. It's the mirror image of cloning: the explorer creates repositories that don't exist yet, while workspaces reconciles ones that already do.
23	
24	### No dedicated screen
25	
26	Unlike cloning, which opens a selection list because its rows don't exist until the clone runs, sync has nothing new to show — every repository is already a row on screen. So sync decorates existing rows instead of opening a new view: a spinner appears in the row's Git Status cell, the same way a running scan shows in the Scanned cell, and the row's data refreshes once the sync completes.
27	
28	### Progress vs. summary are different kinds of information
29	
30	A batch sync updates many rows over time — that's an ongoing *state*, recomputed every frame from the underlying job registry. A completion message ("12 repositories synced"), by contrast, is a one-time *event*. Conflating the two used to mean a progress line could be posted when the first repository started and then silently expire (footer messages have a fixed lifetime) while the ninth repository was still fetching. Splitting them fixes that: progress is derived continuously, and the summary is posted once, when the whole batch settles.
31	
32	### What "sync everything under here" means
33	
34	Scan and sync share one targeting rule instead of each getting a separate selection mode: pressing the key on a git repository acts on that repository; pressing it on a plain directory acts on every repository nested underneath, at any depth; anything else does nothing. One rule for two actions is simpler to learn, and their shortcuts appear and disappear together.
35	
36	The recursive walk stops as soon as it finds a repository — so a repository's own `node_modules` is never descended into. That pruning does the real work of keeping the walk cheap; an artificial depth limit isn't needed once the walk already stops at repository boundaries. The walk also follows Windows junctions/symlinks correctly (checking the actual target rather than trusting `IsDir()` on the link itself), with a cycle guard based on comparing files rather than resolved paths, since path resolution doesn't reliably unwind a junction.
37	
38	A repository is recognized by *inspecting the directory's own listing* rather than by `os.Stat`-ing a fixed `.git` path — this also catches bare repositories (which have `HEAD`, `objects`, and `refs` at the root, but no `.git`), which would otherwise be silently skipped as scan/sync targets.
39	
40	### Partial reads are surfaced, not swallowed
41	
42	If a directory can't be read during the walk, that failure is counted, not silently dropped. The count reaches the screen two ways: a warning is shown when a scan or sync ran on a tree that could only be partly read, and a directory where *nothing* was found because reading failed gets a distinct "couldn't check" message rather than being reported as having no repositories. The reasoning: not being able to look somewhere is not the same claim as having looked and found nothing.
43	
44	### Sync refuses more than it does
45	
46	`git.Sync` is conservative by design — every refusal is deliberate, not a missing feature:
47	
48	| Situation | Result |
49	|---|---|
50	| Behind, clean, no local commits | Fast-forwarded |
51	| Nothing to pull | Reported up to date — unpushed local commits don't change this; sync is strictly the pull direction |
52	| Local commits the remote lacks | Skipped: "diverged — N commits ahead" |
53	| Uncommitted changes (including untracked) | Skipped: "uncommitted changes" |
54	| Detached HEAD, or no upstream configured | Skipped, with the reason named |
55	| Remote unreachable | Reported as failed (distinct from "skipped" — the repository's state relative to its owner's intent is unknown) |
56	
57	There is no merge, no rebase, no stash, and never a push. A divergence between local and remote history is a decision about someone's unpublished work; a tool that guesses at resolving it risks destroying hours of work irreversibly.
58	
59	Notably, the fetch against the remote always runs first, regardless of what the sync ultimately decides to do — because the "how far behind" count comes from a *local* tracking ref that's only accurate immediately after a fetch. This means even a repository whose sync is declined (diverged, dirty, etc.) still has its ahead/behind counts refreshed, because the network round-trip already happened.
60	
61	### Mutual exclusion
62	
63	A repository is never scanned and synced at the same time, and neither operation runs on a repository that's mid-deletion: a scan reads the working tree while a fast-forward rewrites it, and running both would produce a report describing a tree that no longer exists by the time you read it. A single "is this path busy" check, backed by the application's shared job registry, guards scan, sync, and delete against each other — including jobs started from *other* views (e.g., a scan launched from the security view is visible to workspaces' guard too, because both read the same registry rather than each view tracking its own state).
64	
65	### Credentials stay scoped to the configured host
66	
67	The token used for git operations is only ever attached when the repository's remote host matches the configured forge host. A workspaces tree can hold clones from anywhere — GitHub, a client's self-hosted Gitea, a path on a network share — and attaching a personal access token to every outbound request regardless of destination would leak that token to unrelated hosts. This is also why the generic git-sync logic lives in its own package rather than inside the GitLab-specific integration: keeping the two separate avoids a default where a credential could leak by omission.
68	
69	## What the "Scanned" column means
70	
71	The `N/M` count on a directory row is **settled coverage** — how many of the nested repositories have a cached scan result — not live progress. It used to try to be both: during a batch scan, the same cell counted up in real time, which made a mid-batch `3/12` ambiguous (nine remaining? nine never scanned?) shown in a cell far from where the user was looking. Now the cell simply stops counting and spins while a scan is running underneath it, and progress is reported where batch progress belongs: the footer.
72	
73	The footer message for a batch has three forms, and the third is a deliberate concession:
74	
75	```
76	Scanning — 3/12                      one kind of job, started from here
77	Scanning — 3/12 · Syncing — 1/4      two kinds, both started from here
78	3 jobs running — see job list        mixed, or started elsewhere
79	```
80	
81	A single line can't meaningfully summarize four batches launched from three different views, so when it can't identify the specific jobs, it says so honestly rather than showing a partial, misleading count.
82

1	# Keybindings
2	
3	DevDesk's keyboard vocabulary has one rule at its core: **no bare letter is
4	navigation.** Arrow keys and `Tab`/`Shift+Tab` navigate; a lowercase letter
5	is always a local filter or toggle, an uppercase letter is always a
6	resource action, and there are no vim-style `hjkl` aliases.
7	
8	## Navigation
9	
10	| Key | Action |
11	|---|---|
12	| `↑` / `↓` | Move up/down in a list or table |
13	| `PageUp` / `PageDown` | Scroll by page |
14	| `Home` / `End` | Go to top / bottom |
15	| `Tab` / `Shift+Tab` | Move between breadcrumb tabs |
16	| `←` | Go back to the parent level (drill up) |
17	| `→` | Enter the selected group/directory (drill down) |
18	| `Enter` | Select / confirm (in selection mode) |
19	| `Esc` | Go back to the parent level, or cancel/close a modal |
20	
21	## Resource actions — uppercase, same meaning everywhere
22	
23	| Key | Action | Key | Action |
24	|---|---|---|---|
25	| `N` | Create | `E` | Edit |
26	| `D` | Delete | `M` | Rename (*mv*) |
27	| `S` | Scan | `A` | Scan all |
28	| `F` | Refresh (*fetch*) | `C` | Clone selector |
29	| `T` | Terminal | `O` | Open in IDE |
30	| `W` | Open in browser | `L` | Logs |
31	| `V` | Pager | `K` | Stop / kill |
32	| `P` | Prune | `B` | Registry browser |
33	| `G` | Pull (*get*) | `U` | Login / logout |
34	| `X` | Exclude | `R` | MR · PR |
35	| `I` | Issues | `Y` | Copy path |
36	
37	Two declared exceptions to "uppercase for actions": `o` (open the resolved
38	CI pipeline, security/results/CI tab only) and `ctrl+y` (copy the `docker
39	run` command) — narrow enough that reserving a global uppercase for either
40	would cost more than it buys.
41	
42	## Lowercase — local filters and toggles, view by view
43	
44	Lowercase letters never modify anything; they're local and can repeat
45	across views. Examples: `r`/`p`/`s`/`t`/`z` in Containers are cumulative
46	state filters; `c`/`h`/`m`/`l` in Security are cumulative severity filters;
47	`t`/`u`/`l`/`e`/`n`/`z` in Network Diagnostics filter protocol/state. Each
48	view declares its own set — see `internal/ui/keymap` for the full,
49	per-view list.
50	
51	## Global
52	
53	| Key | Action |
54	|---|---|
55	| `ctrl+p` | Open command mode — from anywhere, including inside a focused field |
56	| `:` | Open command mode too, except while editing a text field |
57	| `/` | Search / filter |
58	| `?` | Open help |
59	| `q` | Quit view/app |
60	| `ctrl+r` | Refresh — nothing else |
61	
62	Only three `Ctrl` combinations exist in the whole app: `ctrl+c` (SIGINT),
63	`ctrl+r` (refresh), `ctrl+p` (command line). Most other `Ctrl` letters are
64	already claimed by the terminal, `screen`, or `tmux` (`ctrl+a`, `ctrl+b`,
65	flow control on `ctrl+s`/`ctrl+q`, and `ctrl+i`/`m`/`j`/`h` are literally
66	Tab/Enter/LF/Backspace), so a fourth would be reclaiming ground `Shift`

1	# Configure a context
2	
3	A context is a complete, isolated configuration — forge credentials,
4	workspaces directory, registry, scan settings. Use several when you switch
5	between environments (work, personal, a client) and don't want their
6	settings or credentials to mix.
7	
8	## Create a new context
9	
10	Open the command palette (`ctrl+p`) and go to the **Configuration** view
11	(`:config`), or:
12	
13	```
14	:ctx my-context
15	```
16	
17	`ctx <name>` switches to a context, creating it with defaults if it doesn't
18	exist yet. Context names must be `default` or match `^[a-z0-9-]+$` —
19	lowercase letters, digits, hyphens.
20	
21	## Where it lives on disk
22	
23	| Context    | File                              |
24	| ---------- | ---------------------------------- |
25	| `default`  | `~/.devdesk/config.yaml`           |
26	| any other  | `~/.devdesk/config-<name>.yaml`    |
27	
28	The active context's name is tracked in `~/.devdesk/.current-context`.
29	
30	## List and switch
31	
32	```
33	:context list      # show every context
34	:ctx work          # switch to "work"
35	```
36	
37	## Edit settings
38	
39	Everything under `app:`, `forge:`, `registry:`, `scan:`, `network:`, `mcp:`
40	is editable from the **Configuration** view (`:config`) — closed-set fields
41	(like `forge.type`) cycle with `←/→`, the rest are text fields. See the
42	[configuration reference](../reference/configuration.md) for every key, or
43	edit the YAML file directly and restart.
44	
45	## Credentials stay out of the file
46	
47	Forge tokens and registry passwords are never written to `config.yaml`.
48	DevDesk picks one credential backend per context — the host's keyring first,
49	falling back to the git credential helper, then in-memory only as a last
50	resort that doesn't survive a restart. `app.secret_backend` pins the choice
51	(`auto`, `keyring`, `git-credential`) if the default order isn't what you
52	want.
53	
54	## Set the workspaces directory
55	
56	```yaml
57	app:
58	  workspaces_dir: ~/workspaces   # the default
59	```
60	
61	This is what the **Workspaces** view scans for local git repositories, and
62	where the forge explorer clones into by default.
63

1	# Install DevDesk
2	
3	## Requirements
4	
5	- Go 1.25.5+
6	- A terminal with [Nerd Font](https://www.nerdfonts.com/) support — DevDesk
7	  uses icons throughout the UI; without one, boxes or missing glyphs appear
8	  instead of icons.
9	- Optional, and only if you want the feature: [Trivy](https://trivy.dev/)
10	  (CVE/misconfiguration scanning), [Gitleaks](https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks)
11	  (secret detection), Docker (container management, image scanning). DevDesk
12	  degrades gracefully when any of these is absent — the views that need them
13	  say so rather than failing.
14	
15	## Build from source
16	
17	```bash
18	git clone https://github.com/anthnel/devdesk.git
19	cd devdesk
20	
21	mise run build      # → bin/dk
22	./bin/dk
23	```
24	
25	No `mise`? Plain Go works too:
26	
27	```bash
28	go build -o bin/dk .
29	```
30	
31	## Install to your `$GOPATH/bin`
32	
33	```bash
34	mise run install    # → dk, on your PATH if $GOPATH/bin is
35	```
36	
37	## Verify the build
38	
39	```bash
40	./bin/dk
41	```
42	
43	then, inside the app, `:about` (or `:version`) — it reports the exact
44	version, commit and build date that were stamped into the binary at build
45	time.
46	
47	!!! tip "Windows"
48	    Tasks that use POSIX shell syntax declare `shell = "bash -c"` in
49	    `mise.toml`, so they need Git Bash — it ships with
50	    [Git for Windows](https://gitforwindows.org/).

1	# Your first session
2	
3	This walks through installing DevDesk, launching it, and running your first
4	security scan against a local repository. By the end you will have a working
5	`~/.devdesk/` context and know your way around the command palette.
6	
7	## 1. Install
8	
9	You need Go 1.25.5+ and a terminal with [Nerd Font](https://www.nerdfonts.com/)
10	support (DevDesk uses icons throughout the UI).
11	
12	```bash
13	git clone https://github.com/anthnel/devdesk.git
14	cd devdesk
15	mise run build      # → bin/dk
16	```
17	
18	No `mise`? `go build -o bin/dk .` works too — `mise` only pins tool versions
19	and wires up the project's tasks.
20	
21	## 2. Launch
22	
23	```bash
24	./bin/dk
25	```
26	
27	The **Dashboard** view opens first. It is a summary — forge stats, Docker
28	usage, tool availability — and every number on it is a shortcut into the view
29	that produced it.
30	
31	## 3. Open the command palette
32	
33	Press `ctrl+p` (or `:` when no text field has focus). Type `workspaces` and
34	press `Enter` — or just type `ws`, its short alias.
35	
36	```
37	:ws
38	```
39	
40	The **Workspaces** view lists the git repositories under
41	`app.workspaces_dir` (`~/workspaces` by default — see
42	[Configure a context](../how-to/configure-a-context.md) to change it). If
43	the list is empty, that directory has no git repositories yet; clone one
44	with `git clone` in a separate terminal, or use `git-explorer` once you have
45	authenticated against a forge (see the next tutorial step for authentication,
46	or skip straight to a scan if you already have a local clone).
47	
48	## 4. Run a scan
49	
50	With a repository selected in Workspaces, press `S` (uppercase). DevDesk
51	runs [Trivy](https://trivy.dev/) (CVEs, secrets, misconfiguration) and
52	[Gitleaks](https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks) (secrets) against it in the
53	background.
54	
55	Press `:jobs` (or `:j`) to watch it run — scans are jobs, not blocking waits,
56	so you can keep navigating while one is in flight.
57	
58	When it finishes, `:sec` (Security) shows the findings: severities, file
59	locations, and remediation notes where Trivy provides them.
60	
61	## 5. What's next
62	
63	- [Configure a context](../how-to/configure-a-context.md) — point DevDesk at
64	  your own workspaces directory, forge, and registry.
65	- [Switch forge backend](../how-to/switch-forge-backend.md) — target GitHub
66	  instead of GitLab.
67	- [Command reference](../reference/commands.md) — every command and alias.
68	- [Keybinding reference](../reference/keybindings.md) — the full vocabulary.

# Network

DevDesk's network diagnostics — reachability checks, the local socket table,
and the network interface list — all run *inside the DevDesk process itself*,
never inside a privileged container. This page explains why that constraint
exists, what it cost to satisfy, and how the diagnostics pipeline is built
around it.

## Why nothing runs in a privileged container anymore

Earlier versions of these views ran diagnostic commands (`ss`, `ip addr`,
`iptables`, and similar) inside containers started with
`--network host --pid host --privileged`. On Docker Desktop, `--network
host` is the namespace of the Linux VM that backs Docker, not the host
machine — so these tools were answering for the *wrong machine* entirely.
Concretely, the socket table listed the VM's own NFS daemons with low PIDs
while none of the actual host's dozens of listening sockets appeared, and
sending a "kill" signal to one of those PIDs killed a process inside the VM
under the impression it was freeing a port on the host. The interfaces view
had the same problem: it showed the VM's `eth0` and `docker0` while the real
machine had a completely different set of adapters (a VPN, a mesh network
interface, two competing default routes) with not one name or route in
common.

Under native Linux this defect didn't exist — the container's host network
namespace *is* the real one — which is exactly why it went unnoticed for so
long: it was correct on the platform it was developed on and wrong
everywhere Docker Desktop is used.

The fix, applied one diagnostic at a time, was to read everything directly
from the DevDesk process using OS-level APIs instead of shelling out to
containerized CLI tools. Nothing in the application requests `--network
host` anymore, which is a checkable way of stating the underlying principle:
**DevDesk never claims to answer for a machine that isn't the one it's
running on.**

## The Diagnostics tab

`internal/netcheck` runs a pipeline against a target: resolve, route, reach,
connect, TLS, HTTP — one stage per step, chained so the UI can name exactly
which question is currently being asked. Earlier versions exposed a set of
checkboxes letting the user pick which tools to run; those are gone, because
which checks make sense follows automatically from the target and from
whatever has already failed.

1	# Configuration & Contexts
2	
3	DevDesk keeps its settings in a per-context YAML file and edits them through a dedicated configuration view inside the TUI itself. This page explains the shape of that schema and the reasoning behind how the configuration view handles editing, validation, and persistence.
4	
5	## The configuration schema
6	
7	Configuration loads from `~/.devdesk/config.yaml`, with its schema defined in `internal/config/config.go`:
8	
9	- **`App`** — global settings: theme, default view, workspaces directory, whether hidden files are shown, which secret backend to use
10	- **`Status`** — monitoring settings: refresh interval, the list of monitored components
11	- **`Forge`** — the platform this context targets: type, URL, and clone settings
12	- **`Registry`** — OCI registry configuration
13	- **`Scan`** — security scanning settings (Trivy, Gitleaks)
14	- **`Network`** — the dials the network diagnostics view runs against (timeouts, ping count, certificate expiry warning threshold, ports refresh interval)
15	- **`MCP`** — the read-only MCP server: whether it's enabled (off by default) and an allow-list of exposed tool names
16	
17	**No secret ever lives in this file.** `GitLabConfig` has no `Token` field and `RegistryConfig` has no `Password` field — both are pushed out to the host's secret store instead (see the credentials management notes in the main architecture docs). This is enforced by the schema itself rather than by convention: there's simply no field to accidentally populate.
18	
19	Configuration is injected into views at construction time, and any change must go through `config.Save()` to actually persist.
20	
21	### Migrating an old schema forward
22	
23	The `Forge` section used to be called `gitlab:`, back when GitLab was the only supported backend. Renaming it to `forge:` reflects that a context now targets a *role* (one platform, chosen explicitly) rather than a fixed implementation, and the section gained an explicit `type: gitlab | github` field — declared, never auto-detected from other clues. A missing `type` defaults to `gitlab`, matching what every config file written before the field existed actually meant.
24	
25	The migration step runs deliberately **first**, before any other default-filling logic touches the `Forge` section. Every other piece of default-filling writes into that same section, so running the migration afterward would find a non-empty block, take a naive field-by-field merge path, and silently drop a user's own customized values (`parallel_jobs`, for instance) that weren't present in the legacy shape. YAML parsing here isn't strict, so a section that fails to migrate cleanly doesn't error — it's silently dropped, which for the forge section would mean a context pointing at no host at all.
26	
27	The migration itself takes two different paths depending on what's already present: if the new `forge:` block is entirely absent, the old block is copied over wholesale, field by field. If both old and new blocks are present, the new values win field-by-field, since they were written more recently and reverting to old values would undo whatever edit produced the current file. The one field handled specially is `IncludeArchived` — a plain boolean can't distinguish "explicitly set to false" from "never set," so it's only carried forward from the old block when the new block is completely absent.
28	
29	A similar rename applies to networking: `network:` used to be called `docker:`, from a time when its only field was the image used for a since-removed OCI connectivity test. `NetworkConfig` today holds only the actual netdiag dials.
30	
31	## The configuration view — `internal/ui/configuration`
32	
33	The view edits every **scalar** setting a context carries, organized into six tabs: `app`, a tab named after whichever forge platform is active (`gitlab` or `github` — not the literal section name), `scan`, `network`, `mcp`, and `status`. List-shaped settings deliberately stay where they're actually used instead of being duplicated here — monitors keep their full CRUD flow in the status view, registries keep theirs in the OCI resources view.
34	
35	Tab navigation and field navigation use different keys by design: `Tab`/`Shift+Tab` moves between tabs, `↑`/`↓` moves between fields within a tab — a tabbed form is the one layout where both keys can have exactly one unambiguous job each.
36	
37	Each editable setting is declared as an entry in a table (`fields.go`) holding a single pointer-accessor into the config struct, rather than a separate getter and setter. A design with roughly two dozen settings each needing a matched pair of closures is exactly what produced copy-paste bugs previously — collapsing to one accessor per field means the code that reads a setting and the code that writes it can't disagree about which field they mean.
38	
39	| Value kind | Control | When it persists |
40	|---|---|---|
41	| closed set of values | left/right cycling | immediately |
42	| boolean | checkbox (space to toggle) | immediately |
43	| text / integer | text input | on blur, **after validation** |
44	
45	A value that fails validation (an unparseable integer, a malformed server address) is reported in the footer and deliberately **not written** — silently coercing an invalid value to zero is exactly how a broken Trivy server address ended up saved to a config file in an earlier version.
46	
47	### "On blur" has to include leaving the view entirely
48	
49	Committing a text field's value used to only happen when the user moved focus with the arrow keys or switched tabs — which meant typing a path and then leaving the view via the command line (`ctrl+p`) never actually applied it. Because the router caches views and doesn't re-run initialization on return, coming back to the configuration view would show the typed value on screen while the file on disk still held the old one — the screen appeared to confirm the change on every visit, which is what made the underlying bug hard to track down.
50	
51	Two things fixed this. First, the view implements the router's `Leave()` hook (see [App Shell & Router](app-shell.md)) — called before any switch away from the view, with a refusal cancelling the switch outright, since only the leaving view's own footer can report a rejected value; reporting it anywhere else would post the message to a screen the user is no longer looking at. Second, `esc` now explicitly commits the focused field rather than falling through and doing nothing, since pressing escape to "close" a field was the single most natural gesture that previously settled nothing at all.
52	
53	### Two settings that don't follow the general pattern
54	
55	- **Theme** applies live as it's cycled through, not on blur — waiting until the field loses focus would mean choosing a theme blind, unable to see it applied.
56	- **Secret backend** commits only when focus leaves the field (not on every keypress while cycling), and switching backends **never migrates an existing secret** between them — an earlier version that copied a token to two backends at once is exactly the kind of dual-write this design avoids reintroducing.
57	
58	### The forge tab
59	
60	The `Forge` field is the first field in the Connection group, positioned above the URL, because everything below it — the URL placeholder example, the valid visibility set, several labels, even the tab's own title and icon — reconfigures itself based on this value, so it needs to be visibly "upstream" of the fields that react to it.
61	
62	Changing either the URL or the platform closes the current client-side session and says so in the footer — one flag covers both settings because the underlying consequence is identical either way: the session was opened against configuration that no longer matches what's on screen. Nothing is revoked and no token is deleted; the user changed an address or a platform, not their credentials.
63	
64	Host detection is deliberately conservative: it recognizes `gitlab.com` and `github.com` specifically and nothing else, since self-hosted instances are the case that actually matters and a host like `git.acme.com` could plausibly be either platform — guessing wrong would be worse than not guessing. Detection re-runs whenever the URL field is committed, but only until the user has explicitly touched the `Forge` field themselves; after that, typing a new URL must never silently override an explicit choice.
65	
66	Changing the platform triggers two follow-on effects, both necessary to avoid otherwise-silent inconsistencies: the field table is rebuilt from scratch (since it's computed from the platform type, and the router deliberately keeps this exact view alive across a save rather than rebuilding it), and a `default_visibility` value not supported by the new platform is coerced down to the most private option it does support — GitHub.com, for instance, has no `internal` visibility, and leaving a stale value in place would mean opening a cycle field on a value that isn't even in its own list.

## Container engine: Docker or Podman

DevDesk drives a single container engine at a time — Docker or Podman — for
image scanning, container management, and OCI resource browsing.
`app.container_engine` (see [configuration reference](../reference/configuration.md))
picks it: `auto` (the default) takes Docker if it's on `PATH` and falls back
to Podman, `docker`/`podman` pin one explicitly, and anything else is read as
a path to a binary. Picking one explicitly is worth doing if both are
installed and you want DevDesk to never guess — a *pinned* engine that isn't
installed is reported as an error rather than silently falling back to the
other one, because the two don't hold the same containers.

Everything DevDesk does through the engine — listing containers, pulling
images, inspecting networks, scanning — goes through one `--format`
invocation shape shared by both; only the binary name, the credential helper
prefix, and the registry auth file location differ per engine. One exception:
the detailed per-image disk usage breakdown (`system df -v`) is Docker-only —
it's read by scraping a fixed-width table at column offsets, and Podman's
output doesn't line up with them, so that specific view is disabled rather
than shown wrong.

The **Dashboard**, **Containers**, and **OCI Resources** views don't need to
know which engine is active; they render Docker Hub pull references with an
explicit `docker.io/` prefix, though, since Podman — unlike Docker — doesn't
assume that registry by default for a bare image name.

## Fuzzy find (`g`)

`g` opens a prompt: type at least 3 characters and a ranked list of
directories anywhere under the workspaces root appears — not just the ones
in the current listing — and `Enter` on one jumps straight there, however
deep. It's a shortcut past manual drill-down for a tree with more than a
couple of levels.

The candidate list is a fresh walk of the whole tree every time the prompt
opens, run in the background so typing stays responsive; the view itself
keeps no tree in memory between prompts. The walk stops at each repository
boundary — a repository is a valid jump target, but its own `node_modules`
or `vendor` never is, the same rule scan and sync already use. Ranking is a
plain subsequence match (typed characters must appear in order, not
consecutively) scored higher for consecutive runs and for a match landing
right after a `/` — so `wsdd` beats a same-length coincidental match buried
mid-path when both contain the letters.

The query field sits in the same footer bar slot as the `/` filter and the
document viewer's `g` (go-to-line) — the same framed rectangle, never two
different implementations of it. It's a lowercase, view-local binding, like
the viewer's own `g`: the jump takes an argument (the query), which is not a
role any uppercase action or the arrow keys can cover.

# Run the setup wizard

`dk setup` walks you through creating a context one question at a time,
instead of hand-editing YAML or clicking through the Configuration view field
by field. It's the fastest way to get a new context running, and the one
thing the TUI can't do for itself: guide a user who has no context yet.

```bash
dk setup
```

This runs standalone — no context is loaded first, so it works even before
`~/.devdesk/` exists at all.

## What it asks, in order

1. **Terminal font check** — shows a handful of Nerd Font glyphs and asks if
   they rendered correctly, before anything else risks looking broken.
2. **Context name** — lowercase letters, digits, hyphens, or `default`.
3. **Secret backend** — `auto`, `keyring`, or `git-credential`; checks live
   whether the choice is actually reachable before you commit to it.
4. **Container engine** — `auto`, `docker`, or `podman`; checks live whether
   the selected engine's daemon actually answers, not just whether the
   binary is on `PATH`.
5. **Theme** — the built-in theme plus, network permitting, any additional
   ones fetched from the DevDesk repository.
6. **Forge** — platform (GitLab/GitHub), instance URL, default
   group/organization, default visibility, clone method, and an access
   token, validated live against the real API before it's saved.

Every step explains itself, and every field except the context name can be
left blank to configure later — the wizard still creates the context either
way. `←`/`→` cycles a closed-set answer, `Enter` confirms and advances,
`Esc` goes back a step (or quits, from the first one).

## What it writes

The wizard calls the same save path the Configuration view uses
(`config.SaveContext`), so the result is identical to configuring by hand —
see [Configure a context](configure-a-context.md) for where the file lands
and how contexts are switched. If a context with that name already exists,
it asks before overwriting.

When it finishes, it reports the path it wrote and any warning (a token that
couldn't be saved, for instance) — then `dk` starts the full TUI against the
context you just created.

| Subcommand | Runs |
|---|---|
| `dk` (no argument) | The full TUI |

59	  helpers instead of assembling layout by hand.

61	  filtered down to nothing, it's still a table with a header and zero rows,

# Entire CLI

Entire records agent work as **checkpoints** — persistent records tied to commits — and tracks **sessions** across worktrees. This skill covers driving its CLI.

## Rule 1: the CLI documents itself — never guess flags

Entire ships a machine-readable help surface that always matches the installed binary:

```bash
entire agent-help                      # command map + when to use each
entire agent-help <command>            # exact flags for the installed version
entire agent-help <command> <sub>      # drill further
entire agent-help <command> --json     # structured output
```

**Read it before composing any non-trivial invocation.** The CLI evolves quickly; a
flag list memorised in a skill file goes stale, the self-help does not. This file
therefore documents *which command solves which problem* and the traps — command
names are stable, flags are not.

If a command errors on an unknown flag, do not guess a variant. Run
`entire agent-help <command>` and read the real surface.

## Rule 2: never ask the user for the repo

Entire auto-detects the repository from the git `origin` remote. You are already
inside it.

- Pass `--repo` **only** to target a *different* repo than the current one.
- Repo slugs take several forms: `gh/owner/repo` (GitHub-backed), `et/proj/repo`
  (Entire-native), plain `owner/repo`, or a ULID.

`entire agent-help` prints the detected repo in its footer — use that to confirm
which repo you are acting on before any write operation.

## Command map

| Need | Command |
|---|---|
| What did the agent do here? | `checkpoint explain`, `checkpoint list` |
| Find past work by meaning | `checkpoint search` |
| Who/what produced this line? | `why`, `blame` |
| Which agent knows this area? | `experts` |
| Session state, stop, resume | `session` |
| Activity summary | `recap`, `activity` |
| Written summary of recent work | `dispatch` |
| Is Entire on? | `status`, `enable`, `disable` |
| Something is stuck | `doctor` |
| Remove local session data | `clean` |
| Settings (telemetry, hooks, backend) | `configure` |
| Install agent hooks | `agent add/remove/list` |
| Raw API call | `api` |
| Orgs / projects / repos / access | `org`, `project`, `repo`, `grant` |
| Auth | `login`, `logout`, `auth` |
| Experimental workflows | `labs` |

## Provenance — the highest-value commands

These answer questions plain git cannot, because they join commits to the prompts
and sessions that produced them.

```bash
entire why <file>:42            # commit + checkpoint + prompt + session behind a line
entire blame <file>:12-20       # git-blame enriched with checkpoint metadata
entire blame <file> --long      # adds agent, model, author, session columns
entire experts <scope-or-query> # rank agent provenance for a code scope
entire experts --staged         # use staged paths as the scope
```

All three accept `--json`. Reach for `entire why` before speculating about *why*
code looks a certain way — it often returns the literal prompt that produced it.

## Search

```bash
entire checkpoint search "fix login"          # hybrid semantic + keyword, current repo
entire checkpoint search "..." --all-repos    # widen scope
entire checkpoint search "..." --code         # search code content instead
entire checkpoint search "..." --json --limit 20
```

Queries support inline filters: `author:<name>`, `date:<week|month>`,
`branch:<name>`, `repo:<owner/name>`, `repo:*`.

Requires `entire login` (GitHub device flow). Run with no arguments for an
interactive picker — **avoid that in an agent context**, pass a query and `--json`.

## Reading a checkpoint

```bash
entire checkpoint list                     # checkpoints on the current branch
entire checkpoint explain <id|sha>         # auto-detects checkpoint ID vs commit SHA
entire checkpoint explain <id> --short     # summary only
entire checkpoint explain <id> --json      # metadata only; never embeds transcript bytes
entire checkpoint explain <id> --transcript # stream raw JSONL transcript to stdout
```

Checkpoint IDs may be abbreviated to any unambiguous prefix. A commit carrying an
`Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer resolves as a positional target too.

`--json` and `--transcript` are deliberately separate surfaces: metadata never
carries transcript bytes. If you need both, make two calls.

## Sessions

```bash
entire session current            # active session for this worktree
entire session list               # across all worktrees
entire session info <id> --json
entire session stop               # interactive without an id
entire session resume <branch>
entire session adopt <id> --from ../other-worktree
```

## Token usage

```bash
entire checkpoint tokens <id>                      # usage + optimization advice
entire checkpoint tokens <id> --agent-brief         # compact next-step guidance for agents
entire checkpoint tokens <id> --compare <baseline>  # qualify a reduction
entire session tokens <id>
entire tokens profile                               # aggregate across checkpoints (labs)
```

`--agent-brief` is the right output mode when *you* are the consumer.

## Reporting

```bash
entire recap --week --view both     # day (default) | week | month | 90
entire recap --static               # non-interactive — required in agent context
entire activity                     # overview + recent sessions
entire activity --commits           # recent commits instead
entire dispatch --since 7d          # written summary of recent agent work
entire dispatch --local --all-branches
```

`recap` opens an interactive TUI by default. **Always pass `--static`** when you
are not a human at a terminal.

## Labs (experimental — surface may change)

```bash
entire review                       # multi-agent review of the branch, judge consolidates
entire review --list                # configured profiles
entire investigate <seed-doc>       # multi-agent investigation to quorum
entire investigate show <run-id>
entire import claude-code           # import Claude Code transcripts as read-only history
```

`entire review` is user-triggered and spawns real agents. Do not launch it on your
own initiative — surface it as a suggestion and let the user decide.

## Traps

**Interactive by default.** `recap`, `checkpoint search` with no query,
`session stop` with no id, `review --configure`, and `experts --tui` open TUIs
that will hang a non-interactive session. Pass `--static`, `--json`, or an explicit
argument. `ACCESSIBLE=1` in the environment swaps TUIs for plain-text prompts and
is a useful fallback.

**`entire clean` deletes work.** It removes session state and shadow branches.
Always `--dry-run` first; treat `--force --all` as destructive and confirm with the
user before running it.

**`entire investigate --issue-link` needs `--allow-untrusted-seed`** to run
non-interactively, because a GitHub issue is attacker-influenced content and the
agents run with permission bypass. That guard exists for a reason — do not add the
flag reflexively to silence the refusal.

**Pushes carry a second branch.** `git push` also pushes `entire/checkpoints/v1`.
A remote `HEAD` may resolve to that branch rather than `main`, which makes web UIs
appear to show "nothing" for the project. Check with `git ls-remote origin`.

**`entire api` is a real authenticated call.** `--to core` hits the control plane,
`--to cell` your home cell. Method defaults to GET, but becomes POST as soon as a
field or body is supplied — an accidental `-F` turns a read into a write. Path
placeholders `{owner}`, `{repo}`, `{repo_id}` are filled from the origin remote.

## Setup and repair

```bash
entire enable --agent claude-code   # non-interactive hook install
entire enable --agent-help-skill    # install Entire's own official agent-help skill
entire agent list                   # installed + available agents
entire status --detailed --json
entire doctor                       # diagnose stuck sessions, disconnected metadata branches
entire doctor --force               # auto-fix without prompting
entire configure --telemetry=false
```

`doctor` covers three known failure modes: metadata branches that share no common
ancestor with their remote, Codex hooks missing a trust hash, and sessions stuck in
ACTIVE (idle > 1h) or ENDED (uncondensed) phase.

Note that Entire ships an official `--agent-help-skill`. If a repo installs it,
prefer it as the authority for that repo and keep this skill for cross-repo habits.

9	## Container engine: Docker or Podman
10	
11	DevDesk drives a single container engine at a time — Docker or Podman — for
12	image scanning, container management, and OCI resource browsing.
13	`app.container_engine` (see [configuration reference](../reference/configuration.md))
14	picks it: `auto` (the default) takes Docker if it's on `PATH` and falls back

17	installed and you want DevDesk to never guess — a *pinned* engine that isn't
18	installed is reported as an error rather than silently falling back to the
